title: Timekeeper: Invention of Marine Chronometer
sourceHeading: Timekeeper: The Invention of the Marine Chronometer

source.filename: Practice 56  IETLS 閱讀練習 - Passage 1.pdf

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Until the middle of the 18th century, navigators could not determine their exact position at sea and therefore faced many risks, including shipwreck and running out of supplies before reaching their destination. Establishing one’s position on Earth requires two essential coordinates, one of which is longitude.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Longitude measures how far east or west a place lies from a reference meridian, unlike latitude, which uses the naturally occurring baseline of the equator. To determine longitude, navigators measured the angle between the Moon’s centre and a specific star—the lunar distance—using a marine sextant, as well as the height of both celestial bodies. A nautical almanac then allowed Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) to be determined. This could be used to calculate longitude because one hour of time difference corresponds to 15 degrees of longitude. Unfortunately, the method depended heavily on weather conditions and greatly inconvenienced crews. Another proposed method used the difference between home time and local time. In theory, calculating longitude was straightforward even in mid-ocean with no land in sight. The key was to know the exact time at home at that moment. But how could a sailor know the home time while at sea?

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The obvious answer was to take an accurate clock set to home time before departure. Comparing it with local time, easily identified from the Sun’s position, would reveal the time difference and therefore the ship’s longitude. In practice, nobody in the 18th century had managed to create a clock that could withstand a ship’s violent movement and fluctuating temperatures while remaining accurate enough for navigation.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In 1714, the British government offered a prize of £20,000, administered by the grandly named Board of Longitude, for a solution. If a timekeeper was the answer—and the prize was not restricted to timekeepers—its error could be no more than 2.8 seconds per day. This was considered impossible for any clock or watch at sea, even under the best conditions.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The prize, worth about £2 million today, inspired John Harrison, a self-taught Yorkshire carpenter, to design a practical marine clock. Early in his career, he worked with his younger brother James. Their first major project was a turret clock for the stables at Brocklesby Park, revolutionary because it required no lubrication. Harrison designed a marine clock in 1730 and travelled to London in search of financial support. He explained his ideas to Edmond Halley, the Astronomer Royal, who introduced him to George Graham, one of Britain’s foremost clockmakers. Graham funded Harrison’s early work on sea clocks. Harrison took five years to build Harrison Number One, or H1. He later pursued alternative designs and produced H4, which resembled a large pocket watch. Despite its remarkable performance, the Board of Longitude withheld the prize until it was fully satisfied.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Harrison’s main competitor for the valuable prize was the English mathematician John Hadley, who developed the sextant. This instrument measures angles, such as that between the Sun and the horizon, to calculate the location of a ship or aircraft. The sextant was also significant because it could help determine longitude.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Most pioneers of the chronometer in that generation were English, but not every achievement was theirs. One important figure was the Lancastrian Thomas Earnshaw, who created the definitive chronometer escapement—the spring-detent escapement—and established the final form and production system of the marine chronometer. His work turned it into a genuine modern commercial product and a safe, practical navigational aid for the next century and a half.
